title: Public WHIP rate-limit map is never pruned and is populated before authentication
test: tests/whipRoutes.test.js: 'a flood of distinct addresses never leaves the limiter holding more than its cap', 'expired entries are pruned after the window without their addresses returning', 'at the cap the limiter evicts an expired entry before a live one', 'at the cap with every entry live the limiter evicts the oldest, and a window reset makes an entry the newest', 'the limiter buckets IPv6 clients by their /64 and leaves other identities as they are', 'the public WHIP router drops the oldest tracked address at its cap and keeps limiting the others', 'the public WHIP router's own IP fallback buckets by the client behind TRUST_PROXY proxies, not by the proxy' (and, passing before and after, 'the public WHIP router's own IP fallback uses the connecting address when no proxy is trusted')
proof: The map was private to createWhipRouter, so the unbounded growth could only be pinned through an extracted limiter: on the unchanged lib/whipRoutes.js the six limiter unit tests failed with "createClientRateLimiter is not a function" (the factory did not exist; there was no cap, no sweep and no IPv6 bucketing to test). Two router-level tests failed on the unchanged code for the issue's own reasons: with a cap of two tracked addresses the dropped address was still limited ('the dropped address counts afresh: the map holds at most two addresses', 429 !== 404, because the old map never evicts), and with TRUST_X_FORWARDED_HEADERS on and TRUST_PROXY 2 a second client behind the same proxies got 429 ('a second client behind the same proxies shared the first one's bucket', 429 !== 404, because the default getClientIp was the raw socket address). 8 of 41 tests in tests/whipRoutes.test.js failed before the fix, none after. After the fix: createClientRateLimiter keeps at most MAX_TRACKED_RATE_LIMIT_CLIENTS (10000) entries, sweeps expired entries at most once per window whoever calls (so addresses that never return are dropped), evicts the oldest entry at the cap (an expired one whenever there is one), deletes and re-inserts a key whose window reset so insertion order follows window end, and buckets IPv6 clients by /64 (IPv4-mapped addresses count as their IPv4 address). The router's default getClientIp is now proxy-aware like the WHEP and socket fallbacks (TRUST_PROXY hop count, CF-Connecting-IP only under TRUST_CLOUDFLARE_CONNECTING_IP). VAL-055: server.js already mounts the public router with getClientIp: getRequestClientIp (server.js, in the PUBLIC_WHIP_ENABLED block after createWhipRouter(result.router, ...) with publicEndpoint: true), which resolves the trusted client through lib/requestIdentity.js, so no server.js change was needed. The pre-auth check, the 429 after PUBLIC_WHIP_RATE_LIMIT_MAX attempts, the config defaults and the non-public router are unchanged; the existing 'public WHIP enforces per-IP and global pending-start limits' test passes untouched. node --test tests/whipRoutes.test.js 41/41, tests/expiringTracker.test.js 1/1, npm test 1294/1294, lint and typecheck clean. Commit on lane/server (see TASK-040.md).

title: Unbounded public WHIP rate limiting map leaks memory across unique IP addresses
test: tests/whipRoutes.test.js: 'a flood of distinct addresses never leaves the limiter holding more than its cap', 'expired entries are pruned after the window without their addresses returning', 'the public WHIP router drops the oldest tracked address at its cap and keeps limiting the others'
proof: Same change as C-f04e9d9c1539. On the unchanged code the two limiter tests failed with "createClientRateLimiter is not a function" (no bounded limiter existed) and the router test failed with 'the dropped address counts afresh: the map holds at most two addresses' (429 !== 404): the old map kept every address for the life of the process. After the fix a flood of 500 distinct /64s into a limiter capped at 50 never holds more than 50 entries, 10025 distinct addresses into the default limiter leave exactly 10000, and after the window one later attempt by any address sweeps the 20 expired entries out without their addresses returning. A direct timing run of 300000 distinct /64s through the default limiter ended with size 10000 in about 2.7 s (about 9 microseconds per attempt).
